column1: Salary may come from salt
column2: The word comes from the Latin "salarium". A popular story says Roman soldiers were paid in salt, though historians say the link is uncertain.

column1: Goodbye means "God be with you"
column2: The word is a contraction of the 16th-century phrase "God be with ye". Over time it shortened, influenced by "good day".

column1: Nice used to mean foolish
column2: In Middle English, "nice" meant silly or ignorant, from the Latin "nescius". Its meaning shifted many times before becoming "pleasant".
column3: Words can flip their meaning entirely.

column1: Quarantine comes from forty days
column2: In 14th-century Venice, ships from plague areas had to wait 40 days before landing. The Italian "quaranta giorni" means forty days.

column1: English has no official regulator
column2: Unlike French, which has the Académie française, English has no official body deciding its rules. Dictionaries record usage rather than dictate it.
column3: English grows by use, not decree.

column1: Robot comes from a Czech play
column2: Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R. introduced the word. It comes from "robota", meaning forced labour.

column1: The dot over an i is called a tittle
column2: The small mark over a lowercase i or j is a tittle. It is thought to be where the phrase "to a T" may come from, though that is debated.

column1: Muscle means little mouse
column2: It comes from the Latin "musculus", little mouse. Romans thought flexing muscles looked like mice moving under the skin.
column3: Body words are full of animal pictures.

column1: Disaster means bad star
column2: It comes from the Italian "disastro", from "dis" (bad) and "astro" (star). Disasters were once blamed on the stars.

column1: Clue comes from a ball of thread
column2: A "clew" was a ball of yarn. In Greek myth, Theseus used thread to find his way out of the labyrinth, so a clew became something that guides you.

column1: Shakespeare is credited with many new words
column2: Words like "lonely", "swagger" and "bedroom" first appear in print in his works. Some may simply have been recorded first by him.
column3: First written is not always first said.

column1: OK started as a joke
column2: In 1839, Boston newspapers had a fad for comic abbreviations. "OK" stood for "oll korrect", a deliberate misspelling of "all correct".

column1: Hawaiian has a 13-letter alphabet
column2: The Hawaiian alphabet uses five vowels and eight consonants, including the ʻokina glottal stop. Words often repeat sounds.
column3: Small alphabets can carry rich languages.

column1: Sabotage may come from shoes
column2: One theory says it comes from the French "sabot", a wooden clog, linked to workers clumping or disrupting work. The exact origin is debated.
column3: Etymology is often a best guess.

column1: Avocado comes from an Aztec word
column2: The Nahuatl word "āhuacatl" was adapted by Spanish speakers into "aguacate", which became "avocado" in English.

column1: The longest English word in major dictionaries is a lung disease
column2: Pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis has 45 letters. It was coined in 1935, partly to be the longest word.
column3: Some words exist just to be records.

column1: Bless you is said in many languages
column2: Many cultures have a response to sneezing, such as "Gesundheit" in German, meaning health. The customs probably grew from wishing good health.

column1: Handicap came from a betting game
column2: Hand in cap was a 17th-century trading game. It later described evening out horse races, then disadvantages in general.
column3: Words travel far from their origins.

column1: Ketchup may come from a fish sauce
column2: One theory traces it to a Hokkien Chinese word for a fermented fish sauce. Tomatoes were added much later.

column1: Some languages have no words for left and right
column2: Guugu Yimithirr in Australia uses compass directions instead, such as north and south. Speakers keep a constant sense of orientation.
column3: Language can shape how we think about space.

column1: Alphabet comes from its first two letters
column2: It comes from Greek "alpha" and "beta", the first two letters of the Greek alphabet. The Greeks adapted them from Phoenician letters.

column1: Hazard came from a dice game
column2: Hazard was a medieval dice game, likely from an Arabic word for dice. The meaning shifted from chance to danger.

column1: The ampersand was once a letter
column2: & comes from a ligature of "et", Latin for "and". Children once recited it at the end of the alphabet as "and per se and".

column1: Deadline was once a real line
column2: In the American Civil War, a deadline was a boundary in some prison camps that prisoners could not cross. Later it moved into printing and journalism.
column3: Some everyday words have dark origins.

column1: Mandarin uses tones to change meaning
column2: In Mandarin, the syllable "ma" can mean mother, hemp, horse or scold, depending on its tone. There are four main tones plus a neutral one.
